lesson.title: Speaking Both Languages at Once: How Dual Stack Actually Works
lesson.summary: Dual stack runs complete IPv4 and IPv6 protocol implementations side by side on the same device, each with its own address, letting the device negotiate with each peer over whichever protocol that peer supports.
lesson.body:
Dual stack, introduced briefly as one of the core transition strategies, deserves a closer look because it is the approach most operating systems, routers, and networks default to today. A dual-stack device runs two complete, independent network-layer stacks at once: a full IPv4 implementation with its own IPv4 address, and a full IPv6 implementation with its own IPv6 address, both bound to the same physical or logical interface. The two stacks do not merge or translate into each other in any way; they are simply two parallel systems, each handling its own kind of traffic from the network layer up through the transport layer, sharing only the underlying hardware or link.

When a dual-stack device wants to communicate with another host, it needs to decide which protocol to use, and that decision usually happens through DNS. A dual-stack-capable domain name typically has both an A record, holding an IPv4 address, and an AAAA record, holding an IPv6 address. When a dual-stack client looks up that name, it receives both records and, following a preference approach commonly known in practice as Happy Eyeballs, it will generally attempt an IPv6 connection first, since IPv6 is the preferred long-term protocol, but fall back quickly to IPv4 if the IPv6 attempt fails or is noticeably slower, keeping the connection experience fast and reliable regardless of which protocol actually ends up carrying the traffic.

Dual stack's biggest practical advantage is that it avoids the overhead and fragility of translation or encapsulation: an IPv6 packet is sent as a native IPv6 packet, and an IPv4 packet is sent as a native IPv4 packet, with no extra wrapper header and no translating gateway that has to rewrite addresses in the middle. Every router along a dual-stack path simply needs to support both protocols, forwarding each packet according to its own native header, which is conceptually simpler than the tunneling approach where a router has to know to unwrap an outer header to find the real payload inside.

The tradeoff is that dual stack demands more from network infrastructure up front: every router, firewall, and piece of network management tooling along the path has to be configured, updated, and monitored for two separate protocols instead of one, effectively doubling the surface area for configuration and security policy. A firewall rule written only for IPv4 traffic, for instance, does nothing to protect the same host's IPv6 traffic, a gap that has caused real security incidents where administrators secured a device's IPv4 side thoroughly while its dual-stack IPv6 side sat wide open.

Despite that added complexity, dual stack remains the preferred transition strategy precisely because native, untranslated traffic is more efficient and easier to troubleshoot than anything that requires unwrapping a tunnel or rewriting addresses at a translation gateway, which is why it is typically deployed first, with tunneling reserved for the specific gaps dual stack cannot reach directly.
